newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU spending in 1998 must focus on jobs, EP says.
newsitem.headline: EU spending in 1998 must focus on jobs, EP says.

text.p: The European Union should focus its spending next year on job creating measures, the European Parliament said.
The assembly, which shares power over most aspects of the budget with the Council of Ministers, adopted a report on Thursday evening setting out their priorities for the 1998 budget.

Besides tackling unemployment and social exclusion, and encouraging small and medium-sized enterprises to create jobs, Euro-MPs want the EU to concentrate on preparing its enlargement to the countries of central and eastern Europe, and supporting youth, education and culture programmes.

The parliament's recommendations for fighting mad cow disease and improving the EU's fraud-ridden transit system -- both the subject of parliamentary inquiries -- must also be financed from the 1998 budget, Euro-MPs reminded ministers.

Parliament said ministers would need to make greater efforts in 1998 to keep farm spending, which absorbs about 50 percent of the annual budget and has been vulnerable to fraud and irregularities, at a reasonable level.
This was not just a question of getting more accurate forecasts of the money needed, to prevent the overestimates of the past.
It also required changes to the EU's agriculture regulations so that spending could be controlled more effectively, Euro-MPs said.
This applied to the European Structural Funds too. Euro-MPs were worried by the gulf between the high budget allocations to the funds and the low level of take-up by some member states.
The funds are due for a complete overhaul by the end of 1999 but Euro-MPs want the European Commission to propose ways of tightening up their rules before then.
As for foreign policy, parliament said the EU should spend more on relations with the emerging economies of Latin America.
It must not allow any futher reduction of its aid to the world's poorest countries in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific, Euro-MPs insisted.

Parliament's report, drafted by German Christian Democrat Stanislaw Tillich, indicates a number of outstanding differences with the Council will be back on the agenda when talks on next year's budget begin in earnest this summer.

These include parliament's long-standing demand for a say on farm spending -- over which it has no power, EU financing for areas which are the preserve of the member states like police and immigration, and the arguments over the legal bases of certain budget lines.
